1. Thermal trait: Forest with diverse microclimatic niches can harbour ants favouring both wide temperature range so the foraging ant assemblage would present a wider range of low to high $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ values. In contrast, for rubber plantation without dense canopy, diurnal foragers likely experience a hot thermal landscape and ants with low $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ would be excluded (Bates et al., 2013). Thus, we predict that a significant shift and clustering of $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ trait distribution of ants would be observed from forest to rubber plantation with a higher average $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ of ants in rubber plantation than those in forest (Figure 1b). 2. Occupancy in trait space: Niche differentiation shapes the functional trait space (FTS) of species assemblage (Salas-Lopez et al., 2018). By mapping species traits on different axes within the FTS (Blonder et al., 2014; Hutchinson, 1957), the spatial changes of species assemblages in trait space can reveal the difference of ecological niches between different habitats. Therefore, combining thermal and morphological traits to quantify FTS of ant assemblages of both habitats, we predict that the trait space occupancy in rubber plantation should be smaller than in forest ant-assemblage due to the functional homogeneity in rubber plantation. Additionally, we expect the thermal trait to play a key role in the FTS due to hotter surface temperature observed in rubber plantation than in forest (Figure 1c). 3. Niche structure: Niche structure represents how niche partitioning of species is driven by different functional dimensions within the assemblage. For the specific habitat, rubber plantation presents hotter thermal condition than forest and species would homogenously present higher thermal tolerance. Therefore, the niche partitioning of ant species within rubber plantation should be driven by factors such as resource acquisition and habitat complexity instead of thermal constraints. We expect morphological traits to play a more unique role in niche partitioning of species assemblage in rubber plantation than forest, while $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ should play a more independent role in quantifying FTS in forest ant assemblage (Figure 1d).

Sampling was conducted in Trang province, southern Thailand (7.20–7.60N, 99.65–99.85E; Figure S1a,b) during the dry season from 23rd December 2018 to 9th January 2019 (time from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM). F I G U R E 1 Diagram of the predictions. (a) The habitat characteristics changes in land-use transformation. The functional responses are hypothesised to be dominated by thermal tolerance in three facets: (b) thermal trait, that is, the trait distribution and mean value of critical thermal maximum $( \mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } } )$ in species level; (c) the occupancy of two habitats in trait space and (d) relative roles of traits in niche structuring in two habitats. The trait space is synthesised by both $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ and morphological (Morph.) traits in principal component analysis (PCA) and only the first two components (PC1 and PC2) are shown.

Intraspecific phenotypic plasticity of $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ has previously been demonstrated (Bujan et al., 2020; Gunderson & Stillman, 2015; Sgrò et al., 2016), and intraspecific variation in species’ $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ comparison has often been neglected (Franken et al., 2018). For each ant species, we applied a recently developed statistical tool, trait probability density (TPD), to incorporate intraspecific variation and model trait probability distribution (Carmona et al., 2019) which could enhance our understanding of $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ responses to temperature changes. The functional indices, that is, Functional Richness (FRic) and Functional Evenness (FEve) of a trait belonging to each species, were calculated by using TPD (Carmona et al., 2019). We scaled up the species-level TPD to the who assemblagelevel for each habitat with equal-weighted species abundance and calculated the assemblage dissimilarity between both habitats. Finally, we also tested the relationship between functional indices and average of $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } } .$

We used principal component analysis (PCA) to quantify the FTS of ants. We log-transformed and standardised the mean values of $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ and the six morphological traits (corrected by body size) measured for each species to reduce heteroscedasticity and scale the value to zero mean and unit variance. Next, we excluded the highly correlated morphological traits (pairwise correlation coefficient > 0.5) based on Pearson correlation to avoid unnecessary redundancy, because of unbalanced numbers of traits (i.e., a thermal trait and seven morphological traits). Finally, we produced three FTSs: the first one included all foraging species and investigated the niche occupancy of species assemblages from two habitats within the same regional species pool;

The environmental variables, the average and functional indices of $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ in two habitats were compared by nonparametric Mann–Whitney U test. The difference of species assemblages from two habitats in FTS was tested by Permutational Multivariate Analysis using Euclidian distance matrices. The effect of land-use transformation on $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ at individual level was tested by ordinary least squares (OLS) models for the same species collected from both habitats and by linear mixed effect (LME) model for all individuals with species identity set as a random effect. The effect of land-use on functional traits at species level and trait space at assemblage level was also tested by OLS models (see Table S3).

Temperatures in forest habitat (Figure S1e,f: mean  SD, atmosphere $28.74 \pm 1.60^{\circ}C;$ ground = 26.00  0.88C) are 3.73C and 4.03C lower on average than within rubber plantation for atmospheric and ground surface temperatures respectively (Figure S1e,f: mean  SD, atmosphere = $3 2 . 4 7 \pm 1 . 7 2 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } ;$ ground = 30.03  2.49C). Conversely, humidity is around 20% lower in rubber plantation (Figure S1g: $mean \pm SD , \quad 66.23 \pm 5.21\%)$ than in forest habitat (Figure S1g: $mean \pm SD, 86.71 \pm 6.35\%;$ and canopy openness in rubber plantation is almost 2.6 times larger (Figure S1h: mean  SD, 58.61  12.30%) than in forest (Figure S1h: mean $\pm \; SD ,22.72 \pm 17.92\%)$ . For leaf litter, the depth in forest (Figure S1i: mean  SD, 1.29  0.53 cm) is 2.3 times higher than in rubber plantation (Figure S1i: mean  SD, 0.58  0.34 cm).

Ant species sampled in rubber plantation displayed significantly higher heat tolerances (mean $\pm \mathrm{SD}=48.09 \pm 3.36^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ than in forest $( { \mathsf { m e a n } } \pm { \mathsf { S D } } = 4 5 . 8 0 \pm 2 . 1 6 ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { C } } ) ,$ with an average difference of 2.3C between both species assemblages $(U=94,p=0.0247,n=30;$ Figure 2). The Trait Probability Distribution of $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ at assemblage-level showed that for most ant species $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ values ranged from 41C to $5 1 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } .$

Only two species with individuals collected from multiple sites for each species were collected in both habitats: Anoplolepis gracilipes and Odontoponera denticulata, allowing for intraspecific comparison in their thermal tolerance between populations retrieved in forests and rubber plantations. Forest populations of A. gracilipes showed a significant lower average $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ value by 0.72C than conspecific workers collected in rubber plantations (Figure S3a: $\mathsf { m e a n } \pm \mathsf { S D } \mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ $[ { \mathsf { f o r e s t } } ] = 4 8 . 6 0 \pm 0 . 9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } , U = 9 0 . 5 , p = 0 . 0 2 9 , n = 3 4 ] ;$ forest populations of O. denticulata also showed a similar trend with lower average $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ value by 1.10C than rubber populations (Figure S3b; ${ \sf m e a n } \pm { \sf S D } { \sf C T } _ { \sf m a x }$ [rubber plantation] $= 47.60 \pm 0.66 ^{\circ} C, U = 28.5,$ $p max , relative scape length (RSL) and relative eye position (REP).

For the functional space including species from both habitats (FTS1), the first three components explained over 80% of the variance in the PCA (Table S4 and Figure S7). The first component (accounted for 39.6% of variance) mainly represented by body size (i.e., WL) and REP and the second component (27.5% of variance) was mainly represented by $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ and RMS (Figure 3 and Table S4). Ant assemblages presented similar occupancy and high overlap on the first two components. The third component (16.1%) predominately represented RSL. On the space quantified by the first and third components, ant assemblage of rubber plantation showed significant smaller occupancy than assemblage from forest $( p = 0 . 0 3 )$ . The decrease of FTS occupancy of rubber plantation species was independent to the lower species richness observed there than in forest assemblage (Figure S8).

Trait & Measurement | Hypothesized link to habitat conversion
Body size WL Weber’s Length Diagonal length of mesosoma length | Responds to the habitat complexity, i.e. the size-grain hypothesis (Kaspari & Weiser, 1999); food recourse type and its richness (Silva & Brandao, 2010); heat loss rate about the body size and ambient temperature (Bergmann, 1848).
REW Relative Eye Width Maximum width for the eyes corrected by body size (Eye width / Weber’s length) | Responds to the habitat complexity and allows to detect their predator and prey (Silva & Brandao, 2010).
REP Relative Eye Position (Head width – Interocular distance) / Head length | Responds to the visual ability and diet preference, and species with larger REP are determined as visual predators (Schofield et al., 2016; Sosiak & Barden, 2020).
RFL Relative hind leg Femur Length Maximum length for the femur of high legs corrected by body size (Eye width / Weber’s length) | Determines mobility in terms of foraging for recourses, escaping from predators and heat shock, aggregating for ants (Grevé et al., 2019).
RSL Relative Scape Length Maximum length for the first antenna corrected by body size (Scape length / Weber’s length) | Determines the searching and navigating abilities in responding different niches and adapting different habitats (Silva & Brandao, 2010).
RMS Relative Mandible Size Mandible length / head width | Responds to diet preference of ant predator and environment complexity where should have more species with larger RMS in complex forest habitat due to the foraging specialization hypothesis (Guilherme et al., 2019).
CTmax Critical Thermal maximum | Responds to the ambient temperature and determines species performance in function of temperature (Lutterschmidt & Hutchison, 1997).
